posts.title: Making a Portfolio Agent-Ready: llms.txt, MCP and WebMCP
posts.summary: What I changed so AI assistants can read and query this site: a generated llms.txt, a clear crawl policy, a read-only MCP server on the Worker, in-page tools, and the traps along the way.
posts.content:
A visitor to this site is no longer always a person with a browser. Sometimes it is an assistant that wants to answer "what has this engineer built?" without scraping a page. In November 2026 I spent a week making the site easier for those readers, and this is what changed and what surprised me.

Where it started

An agent-readiness scan scored the site 3 out of 5. The pages were fine for people; for software there was no map of the content, no way to ask a question, and the CDN was blocking AI crawlers before they reached a single file. A re-scan after the work scored 4. The checks that still fail are the ones that do not apply here, such as OAuth discovery, because nothing on the site needs a login.

What I built

  • A map to read first. /llms.txt lists the projects, posts and work history as Markdown links. It is generated from the same JSON files as the pages, so it cannot drift.
  • A clear crawl policy. robots.txt says AI training crawlers are welcome, with Content Signals that state it in a machine-readable way. This was a decision, not a default: I would rather be in the answer than absent from it.
  • A read-only MCP server. The same Cloudflare Worker that serves the live widgets now answers at /mcp. Its tools return the profile, projects, work history, posts, recent GitHub activity and site health numbers. Every tool only reads, and each says so in its annotations.
  • In-page tools. Browsers that support WebMCP get five tools registered from the page itself. The contact tool fills in the form but never sends it.
  • Discovery documents. An API catalog, an MCP server card and an agent skill live under /.well-known/, so a client can find all of the above from the domain name alone.

What surprised me

  • Cloudflare adds its own robots.txt block only while some AI policy is set to block. Once every policy allowed training, the block disappeared, and so did my Content Signals until I moved them into the file in the repository.
  • Adding an MCP handler took the Worker from about 15 KiB to about 1.25 MiB. It still starts fast, but it is a number I now watch.
  • The service worker answered any unknown same-origin request from its cache, which would have served stale API and MCP responses. It needed an early return.
  • GitHub Pages cannot send an extensionless file as application/linkset+json, so the Worker serves the discovery documents on narrow routes.

Use it from Claude

The server needs no sign-in. In Claude, add it as a custom connector (Settings, Connectors, Add custom connector) with the address https://andernet.dev/mcp and sign-in off. In Claude Code, run claude mcp add --transport http portfolio https://andernet.dev/mcp. Then ask it about the projects, the posts or how the site is doing.

None of this uses a model at the moment a visitor loads a page. The site stays static where it can be, and the agents bring their own.

posts.title: How This Site Works: Vanilla JS, WebAssembly, and a Cloudflare Worker
posts.summary: A tour of the architecture behind this portfolio: framework-free ES modules, pages pre-rendered from JSON, a WASM particle hero, a token-based design system, and a Cloudflare Worker for the live parts.
posts.content:
Updated November 2026, after a redesign that changed most of what this post first described.

This portfolio looks like a typical modern web app, but there is no framework underneath: no React, no Vue, and no build step. The production site is plain ES modules served straight from GitHub Pages. This post walks through the architecture and the reasoning behind it.

Pre-rendered first, JavaScript second

The content lives in JSON files: projects, posts and work history. A generator script turns them into real HTML, so every project has its own page at /projects/<name>/, every post has one at /posts/<slug>/, and the project cards, experience and writing on the home page are already in index.html. The site reads fine with JavaScript turned off. A daily GitHub Actions workflow pulls fresh repository data from the GitHub API, regenerates the pages and redeploys, and CI fails if anyone hand-edits generated output.

A short critical path

main.js does only what the first paint needs: the service worker, the theme, navigation and the page shell. Then it signals that the app is ready and starts everything else independently, with sections near the viewport loaded first and the rest when the browser is idle. Nothing optional waits for anything else. By that ready point the home page has made about 14 requests and loaded about 184 KB, and a Playwright test fails the build if the script budget grows.

A WebAssembly particle field in the hero

The animated background behind the hero is a particle flow-field simulation written in AssemblyScript and compiled to WebAssembly. A capability check decides at runtime what you get: capable devices run the WASM simulation, others get a WebGL gradient, and everything else a static CSS gradient. With prefers-reduced-motion on, the animation never starts.

A small design system

Styling is split by page type: core.css is shared by every page, with the home page and article pages each adding one stylesheet of their own. Cascade layers keep the order explicit, and every colour, size and space comes from a token. Each colour token is defined once with light-dark(), so the theme follows your system and the toggle simply flips color-scheme. Stylelint rejects raw spacing and type values. Moving between a project card and its page uses cross-document view transitions, and the command palette (⌘K) and keyboard help are native <dialog> elements.

A Cloudflare Worker for the live parts

GitHub Pages is static, so anything dynamic lives in a Cloudflare Worker answering on the same domain under /api/. It keeps view counts in KV, runs the Turnstile-protected guestbook, caches my recent GitHub activity for the “currently coding” line, counts who is here right now with a Durable Object, and checks the home page every five minutes. Those checks, plus latency and error rates, feed the public status page. Cloudflare also caches the HTML at the edge for an hour and purges it on every deploy.

Readable by agents too

The site publishes an llms.txt, returns any page as Markdown when asked with Accept: text/markdown, and the Worker hosts a read-only MCP server at /mcp so an AI agent can read the projects, posts and work history, and the site’s own stats. In browsers that support WebMCP, the page itself offers a few tools, like searching projects or drafting a contact message (which it never sends).

Kept honest by CI

Every change runs ESLint, Stylelint, Prettier, Vitest unit and Worker tests, a check that every file the site references is actually published, and Playwright end-to-end tests with axe-core accessibility scans. Lighthouse CI audits desktop and mobile on every deploy and fails below 0.9 for performance or 0.95 for accessibility. The site is also an installable PWA with an offline page.

Could a framework do all this? Absolutely. But for a site this size, the browser platform alone turned out to be plenty, and every byte shipped is a byte I can explain.

posts.title: On-Device Gait Analysis with iPhone LiDAR and HealthKit
posts.summary: How I used the iPhone's LiDAR depth sensor and Apple HealthKit to detect walking irregularities without any wearable hardware — all processed on-device with no cloud intermediary.
posts.content:
Most gait analysis systems require dedicated hardware: pressure-sensitive mats, instrumented shoes, or clinical-grade motion capture rigs. The iPhone 12 Pro and later ship with a LiDAR scanner that can produce a dense depth map at 30 fps — more than enough to track the geometry of a walking stride. This post covers how I built a system that uses nothing but the phone itself to flag gait irregularities in real time.

The sensor pipeline

ARKit gives you per-frame depth maps through ARDepthData. The key insight is that you don't need the full reconstruction — just a cropped region of interest at foot height. I extract a ~200×100 pixel slice from the bottom third of each depth frame and track the lowest-point trajectory as a proxy for step timing.

Step events are derived by looking for local minima in the depth signal over a rolling 2-second window. From that you can compute cadence, stride symmetry (left vs. right timing), and coefficient of variation — a standard clinical measure of gait regularity.

Getting the data to a web dashboard

The companion HealthKitBridge iOS app runs a local HTTP server on the device (using Swift's Network framework). The TypeScript web dashboard at health.andernet.dev polls this endpoint over the local network — no internet required, no data leaves the room.

HealthKit is used for ground-truth step counts (the onboard pedometer is extremely accurate) and to pull longer-term trends: resting heart rate, VO₂ max estimates, and walking speed history Apple already captures in the background.

What it can (and can't) detect

The system reliably catches asymmetric stride timing — a common early indicator of hip or knee issues — and large cadence deviations. It's less reliable on carpeted surfaces (the LiDAR reading is noisier) and doesn't handle stairs or slopes well without an explicit classifier. Clinical-grade it is not, but as a personal tracking tool it's surprisingly useful.

Source code for both the iOS bridge and the TypeScript dashboard are on GitHub if you want to dig in.

posts.title: Building a Local-First IoT Dashboard Without the Cloud
posts.summary: Why I stopped routing smart home data through vendor clouds and what I built instead — a local-first dashboard that works even when the internet is down.
posts.content:
Most smart home platforms are cloud-dependent by design. Your light switch sends a packet to a server in Virginia before it turns on the bulb two feet away. Latency aside, it means your home automation goes down when your ISP does, and your usage data lives on someone else's infrastructure.

HomeHub started as a frustration project after my Wemo switches became unresponsive during a 30-minute outage. The goal was a local-first dashboard where the only hard dependency is the local network.

The stack

MQTT is the backbone — it's lightweight, supports publish/subscribe, and has mature client libraries in every language. Eclipse Mosquitto runs in a Docker container on a Raspberry Pi 4. Devices that don't speak MQTT natively get a thin bridge adapter (usually a small Python script).

The dashboard itself is a TypeScript app served locally by the Pi. WebSockets keep state in sync — the MQTT broker broadcasts state changes to the web client via a small Node.js relay. The whole thing works on a phone browser over Wi-Fi, making it a decent control panel without a dedicated touchscreen.

What I learned

The hardest part wasn't the code — it was device onboarding. Every vendor has a different local API story. Philips Hue has a great local REST API. Wemo has a SOAP endpoint (yes, SOAP). Some devices only expose local control after you've authenticated with their cloud once.

For anything new I buy, local API support is now a hard requirement. The Matter standard is making this better, though adoption is still patchy.

The repo is at github.com/and3rn3t/homehub. It's not packaged as a general-purpose tool — it's specific to my setup — but the architecture might be useful if you're solving a similar problem.
